questions.prompt: Show that the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra holds for every quadratic p(x) = ax² + bx + c with real a, b, c and a ≠ 0: p has exactly two complex zeros counted with multiplicity.
questions.prompt_markup: Show that the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra holds for every quadratic p(x) = ax² + bx + c with real a, b, c and a ≠ 0: p has exactly two complex zeros counted with multiplicity.
questions.correct_answer: The zeros are (-b ± √(b² - 4ac))/(2a): two real zeros if D > 0, one real zero of multiplicity 2 if D = 0, two conjugate non-real zeros if D < 0.
questions.required_method: Use the quadratic formula and the cases of the discriminant.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof or derivation. Essential: the formula gives all zeros; the three cases of D = b² - 4ac; for D < 0, √D = i√(-D) is a complex number; for D = 0 the zero -b/(2a) has multiplicity 2 since p(x) = a(x + b/(2a))². Invalid: checking one example.

questions.prompt: A student says p(x) = x³ + x + 1 has no zeros because it does not factor with integers. Use the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra to explain how many complex zeros it has, and explain why at least one of them is real.
questions.prompt_markup: A student says p(x) = x³ + x + 1 has no zeros because it does not factor with integers. Use the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra to explain how many complex zeros it has, and explain why at least one of them is real.
questions.correct_answer: It has 3 complex zeros with multiplicity; non-real zeros of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs, so at most 2 are non-real and at least 1 is real.
questions.required_method: Count zeros by degree; use conjugate pairs for real coefficients.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: degree 3 gives 3 zeros; "no integer factorization" does not mean "no zeros"; conjugate pairs force an odd number of real zeros.

questions.prompt: Prove that every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has at least one real zero.
questions.prompt_markup: Prove that every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has at least one real zero.
questions.correct_answer: An odd number of zeros, minus an even number of non-real zeros, leaves an odd (so nonzero) number of real zeros.
questions.required_method: Count zeros with the theorem; pair non-real zeros.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof or derivation. Essential: n zeros with multiplicity (n odd); conjugate pairs have equal multiplicity, so the non-real zeros count is even; odd minus even is odd ≥ 1.
